pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 6–7 (CONCEPTUAL): understand that 10 can be thought of as a single BUNDLE of ten ones — a 'ten' — and that ten ones can be exchanged for one ten and back. This unitising move (centrality 0.41) is the bedrock of the entire base-ten system.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1–Y2): recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones); non-statutory guidance on grouping in tens.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.NBT.2a '10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a ten'.
• Operational details — the child physically groups ten single cubes into one tens-rod, and reverses it (exchange one ten for ten ones), grasping that '1 ten' and '10 ones' are the SAME quantity named/organised differently. This is UNITISING: treating a group as one thing while knowing it contains ten. It follows teen composition and precedes all multi-digit place value, comparison and column arithmetic.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): group 10 single cubes into one rod and say why. Tier B (6–7): explain that 10 ones is the same as 1 ten. Tier C (7): exchange 10 ones for a single tens block (and vice versa) fluently, using it in a simple problem.
bestPractices: Make the EXCHANGE physical and two-way: swap ten loose ones for one tens-rod and back, so children feel that regrouping conserves quantity — the ten IS ten ones, just bundled.
Use materials that show the ten is made of ten (a rod visibly ten cubes long, a ten-bead bar) BEFORE pre-grouped abstract tokens, so the bundle's tenness is seen, not asserted.
Name the unit deliberately — 'one ten' — and contrast counting 'ten ones' vs counting 'one ten' for the same pile, surfacing the unitising idea.
Link to the teens (prerequisite): a teen number already has one such bundle; now generalise the bundle itself as a countable unit toward decade numbers and two-digit place value.
Foreshadow regrouping in arithmetic: this exchange is exactly the 'carry/borrow' move children will meet in column addition and subtraction.
keyRepresentations: Ten single cubes physically snapping into one tens-rod (and the reverse).
Ten-bead bar / bead string where the ten is one strung unit of ten beads.
Exchange mat: 'ones' column and 'tens' column with a swap action (10 ones ↔ 1 ten).
commonMisconceptions: Thinking a tens-rod is 'one' (counting bundles as single objects), so 3 rods = 3 rather than 30 — the core unitising error.
Believing the ten and the ten ones are different amounts (not conserving quantity across the exchange).
Being unable to reverse the bundling (can make a ten from ones but not break a ten back into ones).
Treating pre-grouped tens tokens as arbitrary symbols without knowing each holds ten.
Confusing 'ten' the count word with 'a ten' the unit.

learn.summary: For children aged 6–7, build the concept that 10 ones can be bundled into a single 'ten' and exchanged back again, with the quantity conserved across the swap. This unitising move — treating a group of ten as one countable thing while knowing it still contains ten — is the foundation of base-ten place value, comparison and column arithmetic. The central activity is a two-way physical/interactive exchange with proportional materials (a rod visibly made of ten cubes) and deliberate naming of the same pile as 'ten ones' or 'one ten'. Supporting activities anchor the equivalence with a reveal, probe reasoning through dialogue, and check retention.

activities.title: Base-ten exchange: bundle and break a ten
feedback: If the child calls a rod 'one', break it apart in front of them and count the ten cubes, then rebuild it: '10 ones make 1 ten — same cubes, bundled up.'
If the child thinks the rearranged amount changed, do it reversibly — build, break, rebuild — counting each time and stressing nothing was added or taken away.
Confirm success when the child exchanges both directions without recounting and names the same pile as either 'ten ones' or 'one ten'.
activities.rationale: Unitising is a physical bundling/exchange action; performing the two-way swap with proportional material lets conservation be felt and directly confronts the 'a rod is one' error. Proportional materials where the ten is visibly ten should precede pre-grouped abstract tokens so the bundle's tenness is seen, not asserted.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils understand that 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a 'ten'.
Year 1–2 pupils recognise the place value of each digit in a two-digit number (tens, ones), grouping in tens.

Unitising — treating a bundle of ten as a single countable unit while knowing it contains ten ones — is the foundational concept of base-ten place value, best built with proportional materials and physical exchange.
learnerActions: Gather ten loose single cubes and join them into one tens-rod that is visibly ten cubes long.
Reverse the move: break (or separate) one tens-rod back into ten loose ones.
Watch or track a running count of the total cubes before and after each swap, and confirm it does not change.
Toggle/say the name for the very same pile two ways: 'ten ones' and 'one ten'.
Respond to challenges such as 'make one ten' and 'break a ten into ten ones, then give me 3 of them — how many loose ones are left?'
activities.intendedInsight: One ten and ten ones are the same quantity, named and organised two ways; bundling or unbundling changes the arrangement, not the amount, and the ten is itself a countable unit.

activities.title: Reveal the ten inside the rod
feedback: If the child guesses a number other than ten, count the revealed cubes together one by one.
Reinforce: 'The rod IS ten ones joined up.'
activities.rationale: A reveal image is a good anchor for the equivalence and counters treating pre-grouped tokens as arbitrary symbols. It is a scaffold: it shows the equivalence but does not let the child perform the exchange, so use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on bundling.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils understand that 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a 'ten'.
learnerActions: Look at a tens-rod shown beside a pile of ten single cubes.
Tap or lift to reveal the rod splitting into ten cubes, with the label 'one ten = ten ones'.
State how many ones are inside one ten.
activities.intendedInsight: A tens-rod is not an arbitrary token: it holds exactly ten ones.

activities.title: Prove it to the doubter
feedback: Accept the full explanation 'they are the same — the stick is ten ones bundled into one ten, so joining them doesn't change how many cubes there are.'
If the child only justifies by counting the loose cubes one by one, nudge toward the bundling relationship: 'What does the stick tell you without counting?'
If the child agrees the rod came from ten but still won't call them equal because 'it looks different now', rebuild and rebreak it, emphasising nothing was added or removed.
activities.rationale: Dialogue can surface and probe the unitising idea and distinguish 'equal because I counted' from 'equal because a ten IS ten ones'. Efficacy of the dialogue medium is not established by the cited sources, so it is proposed as a probe best paired with materials, so the child can act out the proof rather than only assert it.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who claims 'three rods is just three' or 'the loose pile is more than the stick'.
Explain and, if possible, demonstrate why one ten equals ten ones.

Answer probes: 'If I snap the stick back into loose cubes, how many will there be — and how did you know before I did it?', 'Can you make a ten out of these loose ones?', 'If I only had nine loose cubes, could I bundle a ten? Why not?'
activities.intendedInsight: A ten can be counted as one unit that is also ten ones; the learner can justify the equivalence rather than only count.

activities.title: Check the ten-ones equivalence
feedback: For a wrong value, return to the reveal or exchange activity and recount the ten.
activities.rationale: Matching, multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank items are useful for checking whether the equivalence has stuck. Recognition items check retention; they do not elicit the independent bundling and exchange that builds the concept, so use them after hands-on work.
sourceClaims: Grade 1 pupils understand that 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a 'ten'.
learnerActions: Match representations of a ten (ten ones ↔ one ten).
Answer 'a tens-rod is worth how many ones?'
activities.intendedInsight: Confirm the learner reliably recognises that one ten and ten ones are the same quantity.

constraints: Use proportional materials where the ten is visibly made of ten (a rod ten cubes long, a ten-bead bar, a filled ten-frame) before introducing pre-grouped abstract tokens, so the tenness is seen not asserted.
Make the exchange genuinely two-way: bundling ten ones into a ten AND breaking a ten back into ten ones; reversing the bundle is the move needed later for borrowing in subtraction.
Name the unit deliberately as 'one ten' and contrast counting 'ten ones' versus 'one ten' for the same pile.
The reveal image and the recognition quiz are scaffolds/checks: they anchor or test the equivalence but do not let the child perform the conserving exchange that builds unitising.

Checkpoint tiers: (A, age 6) group 10 single cubes into one rod and say why; (B, 6–7) explain that 10 ones is the same as 1 ten; (C, age 7) exchange 10 ones for one tens block and back fluently and use it in a simple problem.

Watch for the core errors: counting a rod as 'one' (so 3 rods = 3), non-conservation across the swap, inability to reverse the bundling, treating pre-grouped tens tokens as arbitrary symbols without knowing each holds ten, and confusing 'ten' the count word with 'a ten' the unit.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Independent re-review found no critical learner-facing errors: arithmetic (1 ten = 10 ones), conservation logic, and medium claims are coherent across all summaries, insights, actions, feedback and constraints.

Source row marked two of three citations as verified:false (the CCSS 1.NBT.2a claim and the NCETM unitising claim); only the DfE National Curriculum claim was verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

The dialogue activity ('Prove it to the doubter') carries no sourceClaim because no cited source supports spoken dialogue as the medium; its efficacy is proposed/untested and it is qualified as best paired with materials.

The legacy source asserted a static image 'can't let the child perform the exchange' and that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing'. These are catalog-fit comparisons, not established efficacy/necessity claims; they have been softened to scoped scaffold/affordance notes. A fixed reveal still teaches the equivalence even though it cannot be manipulated.
Prerequisite reteach IDs referenced in the source assessment (e.g. the internal reteach identifier) are internal identifiers and were not carried into learner-facing guidance.

probeDeeper: If I snap the stick back into loose cubes, how many will there be? How did you know before I did it?
Can you make a ten out of these loose ones? Show me.
If I only had nine loose cubes, could I bundle a ten? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: They are the same. The stick is ten ones bundled into one 'ten', so 1 ten = 10 ones; joining them together doesn't change how many cubes there are.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the ten-stick as a single unit worth one, so the loose cubes look like more: 'there are ten over here but the stick is just one'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Break the stick apart in front of them and count 10; rebuild it. Name it: '10 ones make 1 ten — same cubes, bundled up.' Use exchange games (10 ones ⇄ 1 ten).
errorPatterns.distractor: The loose cubes are more — the stick is only one thing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child points to the stick, calls it 'one', and says the loose pile has more.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks changing the arrangement changed the amount (non-conservation): 'the stick is different so it can't be the same'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do it reversibly: build the stick, break it, rebuild it, each time counting. Emphasise nothing was added or taken away.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're different amounts because the stick looks different.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child agrees the stick came from ten cubes but still won't call them equal because 'they look different now'.

responseLevels.gap: Calls the ten-stick 'one' and judges the loose pile larger, or must recount the stick every time; treats bundle and loose as different amounts.
responseLevels.full: States that 1 ten = 10 ones because the stick IS ten ones bundled, decomposes and recomposes freely, and knows the quantity is conserved without recounting.
responseLevels.partial: Agrees both are ten, but justifies only by counting the loose cubes one-by-one — does not appeal to the bundling relationship.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put ten loose cubes on the table and, next to them, one stick made of ten cubes joined together. Ask: 'Is there the same number of cubes in the loose pile as in the stick — or is one more? How do you know?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has unitised sees the stick AS ten and calls them equal without recounting; a child who hasn't treats the stick as a single object ('one thing') and so judges the loose pile bigger, or has to count the stick cube-by-cube to be convinced. The reason tier separates 'equal because I counted' from 'equal because a ten IS ten ones'.
